# pdm

`pdm` is psdk's download manager: a multi-connection downloader with a
background daemon so transfers survive closing the terminal, resumable
downloads, scheduling, per-URL rules, and shell completion generated
straight from pdm's own flag definitions.

Written in **pure Dart** — no third-party dependency beyond
[`pdata`](https://pub.dev/packages/pdata) for config parsing (YAML/TOML/JSON).
Even checksum hashing (MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256/SHA-512) is implemented from
scratch, with no `crypto` package dependency.

- Repository: [github.com/psdkjoon/pdm](https://github.com/psdkjoon/pdm)
- License: see [License and Contributing](/pdm/license-and-contributing/)
- Current version: **3.1.0**

## Why a daemon?

Downloads started with `pdm add` run through a small background process,
`pdmd`, reachable over a Unix domain socket on Linux/macOS or a TCP loopback
socket on Windows. That means:

- Closing the terminal (or the SSH session) doesn't interrupt a transfer.
- Multiple `pdm` invocations (`pdm list`, `pdm watch <id>`, another `pdm add`)
  all talk to the same daemon and see the same task list.
- The daemon can auto-spawn itself the first time it's needed, or you can run
  it as a proper login service (see [Daemon &
  Service](/pdm/daemon-and-service/)).

If you'd rather block in the current terminal instead — no daemon involved —
add `--foreground` / `-f` to `pdm add`, or use `pdm add --background` to make
the default explicit.

## 1. Install

Grab a self-contained installer from the [releases
page](https://github.com/psdkjoon/pdm/releases/latest). Every release ships
`pdm-linux-x64.exe` (a self-extracting installer, despite the extension) and
`pdm-windows-x64.exe`, plus a `SHA256SUMS` file you should check the download
against before running it.

```bash
# check the download against SHA256SUMS first
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing

sudo ./pdm-linux-x64      # installs pdm + pdmd to /usr/bin
./pdm-linux-x64 --user    # or to ~/.local/bin instead, no sudo needed
```

On Arch Linux there's no AUR package yet — the installer above is the
supported path. It embeds both the `pdm` CLI and the `pdmd` daemon binary,
verifies their SHA-256 against a checksum baked into the installer itself,
and adds the install directory to your `PATH` if it isn't already there.

On Windows, just run `pdm-windows-x64.exe` — it installs itself under
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\pdm` and adds itself to `PATH` automatically (no
admin prompt needed, since it's a per-user install on that platform).

### Uninstalling

The same installer binary can remove everything it installed:

```bash
./pdm-linux-x64 uninstall                # full removal
./pdm-linux-x64 uninstall --keep-config  # keep ~/.config/pdm and history
```

This stops a running daemon, removes the daemon auto-start service
(systemd/launchd/schtasks — see [Daemon &
Service](/pdm/daemon-and-service/)), deletes both the bash and zsh completion
scripts it can find (system-wide and per-user), and — unless `--keep-config`
is passed — deletes your config directory and download state/history
(`~/.config/pdm`, `~/.local/state/pdm`). It checks both the system and
per-user install locations regardless of whether the original install used
`--user`, so it finds pdm no matter how it got there.

### Shell completion

```bash
pdm completion            # auto-detects bash/zsh from $SHELL
pdm completion bash       # explicit
pdm completion zsh
```

See [Shell Completion](/pdm/shell-completion/) for how it works and what it
can and can't offer on each shell.

## 2. Core concepts

A few names come up everywhere in pdm's docs and `--help` output:

- **Task** — one download, identified by an 8-character lowercase
  alphanumeric id (e.g. `a3f9k2m1`), assigned when you `pdm add` it. See
  [Task Lifecycle](/pdm/task-lifecycle/) for the full status list and
  transitions.
- **Segment** — a byte range of a task's file. When the server supports
  `Range` requests, pdm splits the file into up to `--connections` segments
  and downloads them concurrently; each segment tracks its own progress so a
  paused/interrupted download resumes only the unfinished ranges. See
  [Multi-Connection Downloads &
  Resume](/pdm/multi-connection-downloads-and-resume/).
- **Daemon (`pdmd`)** — the background process that actually runs
  tasks. `pdm` (the CLI) is a thin client that talks to it over a socket,
  except in `--foreground` mode where the CLI runs the download itself with
  no daemon involved.
- **Rule** — a regex-based override in the config file that changes
  options (save directory, connections, proxy, etc.) for URLs matching a
  pattern, checked top to bottom. See
  [Configuration](/pdm/configuration/#per-url-rules).
- **Schedule** — a task can be set to start at a specific time
  (`--at`), repeat on an interval (`--every`), or wait for the next daemon
  startup (`--on-startup`). See
  [Scheduling](/pdm/scheduling/).

## 3. First download

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/big-file.iso
```

This queues the download with the daemon (auto-spawning it if it isn't
already running) and returns immediately:

```
Added a3f9k2m1 (running in background). Use "pdm watch a3f9k2m1" to follow progress.
```

Follow along, list everything, or block until it's done:

```bash
pdm watch a3f9k2m1         # live progress bar for one task
pdm list                   # table of every task and its status
pdm add <url> -f           # add AND block here with a progress bar instead
```

`pdm help <command>` prints the full flag list for any command — every flag
has both a short and a long form (e.g. `-c` / `--connections`). See [CLI
Overview](/pdm/cli-overview/) for global flags shared by every command, or
jump straight to [Commands add](/pdm/commands-add/) and the other command
pages under **Guides**.

## 4. As a library

pdm's core is a normal Dart package with no CLI dependency — `lib/src/*.dart`
has no awareness of flags or terminal output; only `lib/src/cli/*.dart`
does. That means you can depend on `pdm` from your own Dart code and drive
downloads programmatically:

```dart
import 'package:pdm/pdm.dart';

final manager = DownloadManager();
manager.add(
  'https://example.com/file.iso',
  options: const TaskOptions(connections: 8, retries: 5),
  schedule: Schedule(every: Duration(days: 1)),
);
```

See [Using pdm as a Dart Library](/pdm/using-pdm-as-a-dart-library/) in the
API Reference section for the full exported surface and usage patterns.

# Requirements and Platforms

## Dart SDK

Building pdm from source requires Dart SDK `^3.5.0` (see `pubspec.yaml`'s
`environment.sdk` constraint). If you're only installing a released binary,
no Dart SDK is needed at all — the release installers are self-contained.

## Supported platforms

pdm targets Linux, macOS, and Windows. Platform differences that show up in
the docs:

| Area | Linux / macOS | Windows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daemon transport | Unix domain socket | TCP loopback (`127.0.0.1`) |
| Default socket/host | `~/.local/state/pdm/pdm.sock` (`$XDG_STATE_HOME/pdm` if set) | `--daemon-host` / `--daemon-port`, default `127.0.0.1:7420` |
| Default config path | `~/.config/pdm/pdm.yaml` | `%APPDATA%\pdm\pdm.yaml` |
| Auto-start service | systemd `--user` unit (Linux) / launchd agent (macOS) | Scheduled Task (`schtasks`, runs on logon) |
| `--on-complete` built-ins | `systemctl`/`pmset`/`loginctl` (see [On-Complete Hooks](/pdm/on-complete-hooks/)) | `shutdown.exe`, `rundll32.exe` |
| Default install dir | `/usr/bin` (system) or `~/.local/bin` (`--user`) | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\pdm` |
| Notifications | `notify-send` (Linux) / `osascript` (macOS) | `msg` |

Since you're on **Arch Linux**, everything above in the "Linux / macOS"
column applies to you directly: the daemon listens on a Unix socket at
`~/.local/state/pdm/pdm.sock` by default, config lives at
`~/.config/pdm/pdm.yaml`, and `pdm daemon enable` installs a systemd
`--user` service rather than anything requiring root. `pdm daemon enable`
runs `systemctl --user enable --now pdmd.service` under the hood — if you've
never used a user-level systemd service before, `loginctl enable-linger
$USER` lets it keep running after you log out.

## Dependencies

Exactly one third-party package: [`pdata`](https://pub.dev/packages/pdata)
`^1.0.0`, used for reading/writing the config file in whichever of
YAML/TOML/JSON you prefer. Everything else — HTTP, checksum hashing,
argument parsing, terminal color output — is implemented directly on top of
`dart:io` and `dart:convert` with no further dependencies.

## Building from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/psdkjoon/pdm.git
cd pdm
dart pub get
dart run bin/pdm.dart --help
```

Compiling a standalone executable (what the release installer embeds):

```bash
dart compile exe bin/pdm.dart -o pdm --define=PDM_VERSION=3.1.0
dart compile exe bin/pdmd.dart -o pdmd --define=PDM_VERSION=3.1.0
```

`--define=PDM_VERSION=...` bakes the version string in at compile time so
`pdm version` reports correctly even though a compiled binary has no
`pubspec.yaml` next to it to read from — see [`pdm
version`](/pdm/commands-misc/#pdm-version) for why that matters.

# Configuration

pdm reads a single config file that supplies defaults for every command.
**CLI flags always win over the config file, and the config file always wins
over pdm's built-in defaults.**

## File location

| Source | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Default (Linux/macOS) | `~/.config/pdm/pdm.yaml` |
| Default (Windows) | `%APPDATA%\pdm\pdm.yaml` |
| Override | `$PDM_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable |
| Per-command override | `--config <path>` / `-g <path>` (any pdm command) |

The format is inferred from the file extension — `.yaml`/`.yml`, `.toml`, or
`.json` — via [`pdata`](https://pub.dev/packages/pdata). If no config file
exists at the resolved path, pdm silently falls back to its built-in
defaults; it does not create one for you automatically.

Generate a starting file with the built-in defaults:

```bash
pdm config dump --output ~/.config/pdm/pdm.yaml
pdm config dump --format toml --output ~/.config/pdm/pdm.toml
pdm config dump                       # print YAML to stdout, don't write
```

See [`pdm config`](/pdm/commands-misc/#pdm-config-dump) for the full flag
list of this command.

## Full key reference

Every key is optional; anything omitted falls back to its default. Defaults
shown below are pdm's actual built-in values.

| Key | Type | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `connections` | int | `4` | Default `--connections` for new tasks |
| `maxConcurrentTasks` | int | `3` | How many tasks the daemon runs at once; the rest queue |
| `retries` | int | `3` | Retry attempts per segment before a task fails |
| `retryDelay` | int (ms) | `1000` | Base delay between retries |
| `retryBackoff` | bool | `true` | Exponential backoff (doubles each attempt, capped at 2^10×) vs. flat delay |
| `timeout` | int (sec) | `30` | Connection/read timeout |
| `speedLimit` | int (bytes/sec) or `null` | `null` | Default per-task speed cap; unset = unlimited |
| `globalSpeedLimit` | int (bytes/sec) or `null` | `null` | Cap shared across *all* concurrent downloads, on top of any per-task limit |
| `maxRedirects` | int | `5` | Max HTTP redirects to follow |
| `insecure` | bool | `false` | Skip TLS certificate verification by default |
| `downloadDir` | string (path) | `"~/Downloads"` | Default save directory; `~` is expanded |
| `theme` | string | `"default"` | `default`, `rainbow`, or `catppuccin` — see [Themes](/pdm/themes/) |
| `color` | bool | `true` | Enable ANSI color (also needs a real terminal; see `--no-color`) |
| `daemonHost` | string | `"127.0.0.1"` | Daemon TCP host — **Windows only** |
| `daemonPort` | int | `7420` | Daemon TCP port — **Windows only** |
| `socketPath` | string (path) | `"~/.local/state/pdm/pdm.sock"` | Daemon Unix socket path — **Linux/macOS only** |
| `proxy` | string (URL) or `null` | `null` | Default HTTP proxy for all tasks |
| `proxyUser` | string or `null` | `null` | Proxy basic-auth username |
| `proxyPass` | string or `null` | `null` | Proxy basic-auth password |
| `proxyBypass` | list of strings | `[]` | Hosts (and their subdomains) to bypass the proxy for |
| `onCompleteAliases` | map of string→string | `{}` | Custom `--on-complete` commands — see [On-Complete Hooks](/pdm/on-complete-hooks/) |
| `rules` | list of rule objects | `[]` | Per-URL overrides — see [below](#per-url-rules) |
| `notifications` | bool | `false` | Send a desktop notification when a task finishes/fails |
| `checkDiskSpace` | bool | `true` | Check free disk space before starting a task |

## Example: full YAML config

```yaml
connections: 8
maxConcurrentTasks: 4
retries: 5
retryDelay: 1000
retryBackoff: true
timeout: 45
speedLimit: null
globalSpeedLimit: 10485760   # 10 MiB/s shared across every active task
maxRedirects: 5
insecure: false
downloadDir: "~/Downloads"
theme: catppuccin
color: true
socketPath: "~/.local/state/pdm/pdm.sock"
proxy: null
proxyUser: null
proxyPass: null
proxyBypass: []
notifications: true
checkDiskSpace: true

onCompleteAliases:
  backup: "rsync -a {path} /mnt/backup/"
  notify-webhook: "curl -X POST -d 'status={status}&file={path}' https://example.com/hook"

rules:
  - pattern: "example\\.com/videos/"
    saveDir: "~/Videos"
    connections: 16
  - pattern: "\\.iso$"
    saveDir: "~/ISOs"
    proxy: "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
```

The equivalent as TOML or JSON works the same way — pick whichever format
you like and give the file the matching extension; `pdm config dump
--format toml` / `--format json` will generate one for you.

## Per-URL rules

The `rules` list holds regex-based overrides, checked **top to bottom** —
the first pattern that matches a URL wins, and its fields are merged on top
of the flags/config that would otherwise apply. Unset fields inside a rule
fall through to the normal flag/config value.

| Rule field | Type | Overrides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pattern` | string (regex, **required**) | Matched against the full URL with `RegExp(pattern).hasMatch(url)` |
| `saveDir` | string (path) | Save directory for matching URLs (also accepts the key `dir`) |
| `connections` | int | Connection count for matching URLs |
| `proxy` | string (URL) | Proxy for matching URLs |
| `speedLimit` | int (bytes/sec) | Per-task speed cap for matching URLs |
| `headers` | map of string→string | Extra headers merged into the request |
| `onComplete` | string | `--on-complete` command/alias for matching URLs |

```yaml
rules:
  - pattern: "example\\.com/videos/"
    saveDir: "~/Videos"
    connections: 16
  - pattern: "\\.iso$"
    saveDir: "~/ISOs"
    proxy: "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
  - pattern: "internal\\.corp\\.example"
    headers:
      X-Api-Key: "secret-token"
    onComplete: backup
```

Remember that YAML/TOML/JSON strings need their own escaping on top of
regex escaping — a literal `.` in a pattern needs to become `\\.` in YAML
(one backslash for YAML, one for regex) as shown above.

## Precedence, concretely

For any given option (say, `connections`), pdm resolves it in this order,
highest priority first:

1. The `--connections` flag on the `pdm add` command line, if given.
2. A matching rule's `connections` field, if a rule in `rules` matches the
   URL and sets it.
3. The `connections` key in the config file.
4. pdm's built-in default (`4`).

This is the general pattern for every option that can be set in more than
one place — see [CLI Overview](/pdm/cli-overview/#flag-precedence) for the
short version and [Commands add](/pdm/commands-add/) for exactly which
`add` flags fall back to which config keys.

# Environment Variables

pdm reads a small number of environment variables directly (outside of the
config file's own precedence chain).

| Variable | Effect | Platform |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PDM_CONFIG_PATH` | Overrides the config file path (still beaten by `--config`/`-g`) | All |
| `XDG_STATE_HOME` | If set, state/history live at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/pdm` instead of `~/.local/state/pdm` | Linux/macOS |
| `PDMD_PATH` | Overrides how `pdm` locates the `pdmd` daemon executable to auto-spawn | All |
| `HOME` | Used to resolve `~` in paths and as the base for default config/state dirs | Linux/macOS |
| `USERPROFILE`, `HOMEDRIVE`, `HOMEPATH` | Windows equivalents of `HOME`, checked in that order | Windows |
| `APPDATA` | Base for the default Windows config path | Windows |
| `LOCALAPPDATA` | Base for the default Windows install directory | Windows |
| `SHELL` | Used by `pdm completion` (no argument) to auto-detect bash vs. zsh | Linux/macOS |

## Why `PDMD_PATH` exists

Early versions resolved the daemon binary's location via `Platform.script`,
which only works when running under `dart run` — it's meaningless inside a
compiled executable, which made `pdm daemon enable` and background
auto-spawn (`pdm add` without `--foreground`) fail silently once installed.
pdm now resolves `pdmd`/`pdmd.exe` as a sibling file of the running `pdm`
binary by default (i.e. in the same install directory), with `PDMD_PATH` as
an explicit override for non-standard layouts (e.g. running a locally built
`pdmd` while a released `pdm` is on your `PATH`).

```bash
PDMD_PATH=/home/psdk/dev/pdm/build/pdmd pdm add https://example.com/file.iso
```

## `~` expansion

Every path-shaped config value and flag (`downloadDir`, `socketPath`,
`--output`, `--config`, `--cookie-file`, etc.) has `~` expanded to your home
directory before use. This is pdm's own expansion, independent of shell
tilde expansion, so `~` works the same whether it comes from a quoted config
file string or a flag passed through a script.

Guides.Adding Downloads:
# Adding Downloads

`pdm add` is the entry point for every download. This guide walks through
the different ways to call it; see [Commands:
add](/pdm/commands-add/) for the exhaustive flag table.

## One URL, backgrounded (the default)

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso
```

Queues the task with the daemon and returns immediately once it's accepted.
The file name is inferred from the last path segment of the URL and saved
under `downloadDir` (default `~/Downloads`) unless you pass `--output`.

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso --output ~/ISOs/custom-name.iso
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso -o ~/ISOs/custom-name.iso   # same, short form
```

`--output`/`-o` only makes sense for a single URL — using it with more than
one URL, or together with `--file`, is a hard error (each URL in a batch
needs its own inferred name).

## One URL, blocking with a progress bar

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso --foreground
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso -f     # short form
```

Runs entirely in the current process with no daemon involved — useful for
scripts that want to wait synchronously, or when you don't want a daemon
running at all. `--background`/`-b` is the (already-default) opposite and
exists mainly for explicitness or to override a config-level default.

## Multiple URLs at once

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/a.zip https://example.com/b.zip https://example.com/c.zip
```

Every positional argument after `add` that isn't consumed by a flag is
treated as a URL. In background mode they're all queued in one client
session; in `--foreground` mode they run one after another in the same
process, with a summary line (`Completed N/M downloads.`) at the end.

## Batch import from a file

```bash
pdm add --file urls.txt
pdm add -B urls.txt      # short form
```

`urls.txt` is one URL per line; blank lines and lines starting with `#` are
skipped, so you can comment a batch file:

```text
# Linux ISOs
https://example.com/distro1.iso
https://example.com/distro2.iso

# not today
# https://example.com/huge-file.bin
```

`--file` and `--output` are mutually exclusive (each URL in a batch gets its
own inferred name); combining them is an error.

## Headers, auth, and cookies

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/file \
  --header "X-Api-Key: secret123" \
  --header "X-Client: pdm" \
  --user-agent "Mozilla/5.0 pdm/3.1.0" \
  --referer "https://example.com/" \
  --auth-user psdk --auth-pass hunter2
```

`--header`/`-e` is repeatable — pass it multiple times for multiple headers,
each as `"Key: Value"`. `--auth-user`/`--auth-pass` sends HTTP Basic auth.

For cookies, use one of:

```bash
pdm add <url> --cookie "session=abc123; theme=dark"
pdm add <url> --cookie-file ~/.cookies/example.com.txt   # Netscape format
```

`--cookie-file` wins over `--cookie` if both are given. The cookie file must
be in the standard Netscape/Mozilla tab-separated format (the same one
browsers and `curl`/`wget` use for `cookies.txt` exports); lines are parsed
as `domain, flag, path, secure, expiry, name, value` and only `name`/`value`
are used, joined as `name=value; name2=value2`.

## Skip the queue: start paused

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso --start-paused
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso -x
```

Adds the task in the `paused` state without starting it. Useful for staging
a batch of downloads you'll kick off later with `pdm resume --all`, or for
reviewing `pdm list` before committing bandwidth.

## Duplicate detection

By default, adding a URL (or an inferred/explicit save path) that matches an
existing non-finished, non-canceled task is rejected:

```
Error: Duplicate of existing task a3f9k2m1 (same url or save path)
```

Pass `--allow-duplicate`/`-D` to add it anyway — useful if you intentionally
want two independent copies of the same file.

Guides.Multi-Connection Downloads and Resume:
# Multi-Connection Downloads and Resume

## How segmentation works

When you `pdm add` a URL, the daemon first probes it (`HEAD`, falling back
to a 1-byte `GET Range: bytes=0-0` request if the server doesn't answer
`HEAD` usefully) to determine:

- The total file size (`Content-Length`, or from a `Content-Range` header on
  the ranged fallback request).
- Whether the server supports byte-range requests (`Accept-Ranges: bytes`,
  or a `206 Partial Content` response to the ranged probe).

If both are known, pdm splits the file into up to `--connections` segments
of roughly equal size (the split evenly distributes any remainder bytes
across the first few segments) and downloads them **concurrently** over
separate connections, writing each segment directly to its byte range in the
destination file via random-access writes. If the server doesn't support
ranges, or the size can't be determined, pdm falls back to a single segment
— effectively a normal sequential download.

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/big.iso --connections 16
pdm add https://example.com/big.iso -c 16   # short form
```

There's no hard-coded upper limit in the flag itself, but the effective
segment count is clamped to the file size in bytes (you can't have more
segments than bytes) and, practically, to what the server and your network
can sustain — very high values mostly just increase connection overhead
once you're past what the link and server concurrency limits allow.

## How resume works

Segment progress (`downloaded` bytes within each segment) is persisted with
the rest of the task's state after every progress update. If a task is
interrupted — paused, the daemon restarted, the process killed — its
segments remember exactly how many bytes of each range were already
written. Resuming (`pdm resume <id>`, or the daemon requeuing it
automatically on restart) re-opens the destination file in append mode and
each segment's HTTP request asks only for its **remaining** range:

```
Range: bytes=<segment_start + already_downloaded>-<segment_end>
```

This means resume is exact — no re-downloading of bytes already on disk —
as long as the server still supports ranges for that URL. If a task that
previously had range support somehow doesn't on resume (e.g. the server
config changed), that segment will fail rather than silently
re-downloading from the start.

A task that was `downloading` or `probing` when the daemon last shut down is
marked `paused` on the next startup rather than resumed automatically — see
[Task Lifecycle](/pdm/task-lifecycle/) for the full status transition table,
and [Scheduling](/pdm/scheduling/) for the one case
(`--on-startup`) where a task *does* start automatically.

## Retries and backoff

Each segment retries independently on failure:

```bash
pdm add <url> --retries 5 --retry-delay 2000
pdm add <url> -r 5 -d 2000
```

- `--retries`/`-r`: retry attempts **per segment** before the whole task is
  marked `failed`. Default `3` (from config `retries`).
- `--retry-delay`/`-d`: base delay in milliseconds between attempts on the
  same segment. Default `1000` (from config `retryDelay`).
- By default, delay grows exponentially: `delay × 2^(attempt-1)`, capped at
  a `2^10` multiplier so it doesn't grow unbounded on long-running tasks.
  Pass `--linear-retries`/`-L` to use the flat `--retry-delay` on every
  attempt instead.

If some segments finish and others exhaust their retries, the task is marked
`failed` with `error: "Incomplete download"` (or the specific HTTP/network
error from the segment that failed last) rather than silently keeping the
partial file as `completed`.

## Verifying integrity with checksums

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso --checksum sha256:a1b2c3...
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso -k md5:d41d8cd9...
```

`--checksum`/`-k` takes `algo:hex`, where `algo` is one of `md5`, `sha1`,
`sha256`, or `sha512` — all implemented directly in pdm with no external
crypto dependency. Once every segment finishes, the task moves to a
`verifying` status while pdm hashes the completed file and compares it
(case-insensitively) against the expected hex digest:

- Match → task moves to `completed`.
- Mismatch → task moves to `failed` with `error: "Checksum mismatch"`.
- No `--checksum` given → task moves straight to `completed` once segments
  finish, with no verification step.

## Disk space checks

Before writing begins, pdm checks free disk space against the remaining
bytes needed (total size minus what's already downloaded, for a resumed
task) and fails the task up front — with a clear
`"Not enough disk space: need N bytes, have M"` error — rather than filling
the disk partway through. Disable this with `checkDiskSpace: false` in the
config file (there's no dedicated per-task flag for it; it inherits from
config).

## Speed limiting

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/big.iso --speed-limit 2M
pdm add https://example.com/big.iso -l 500K
```

`--speed-limit`/`-l` accepts a plain byte count or a size with a `K`/`M`/`G`
suffix (case-insensitive, binary multiples — `K` = 1024, `M` = 1024²,
`G` = 1024³), enforced per-task across all its segments combined. This is
separate from `globalSpeedLimit` in the config file, which caps total
throughput across *every* concurrently running task; both can be set at
once and both apply.
Guides.Scheduling:
# Scheduling

Three flags on `pdm add` control when (and how often) a task runs. They're
mutually exclusive in the ways noted below.

## Start at a specific time: `--at`

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/big.iso --at 22:00
pdm add https://example.com/big.iso --at 2026-09-20T03:00:00
pdm add https://example.com/big.iso --at +2h
```

`--at`/`-a` accepts three formats:

| Format | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ISO 8601 date/time | `2026-09-20T03:00:00` | An absolute point in time |
| `HH:mm` (24-hour) | `22:00` | Today at that time, or **tomorrow** at that time if it's already past today |
| `+<duration>` | `+2h`, `+30m`, `+1d` | Relative to now — see the duration units in the table below |

A task scheduled with `--at` shows status `scheduled` in `pdm list` until
its time arrives, at which point the daemon's schedule checker (which polls
once per second) moves it to `queued` and it enters the normal queue.

`--at` conflicts with `--on-startup` — a task can't be both "start at a
specific time" and "start whenever the daemon next boots."

## Repeat on an interval: `--every`

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/daily-report.csv --every 1d
pdm add https://example.com/status.json --every 6h
```

`--every`/`-E` re-queues the task automatically after each successful
completion, `<duration>` after the run that just finished (not on a fixed
wall-clock schedule — each run is scheduled relative to when the *previous*
one completed). Accepted duration units:

| Suffix | Unit |
| --- | --- |
| `ms` | milliseconds |
| `s` | seconds |
| `m` | minutes |
| `h` | hours |
| `d` | days |

`--every` can be combined with `--at` (first run at a specific time, then
repeating from there) but a recurring task's segments, total size, and any
previous error are reset before each re-run, so each occurrence is a fresh
full download rather than a resume of the last one.

## Defer until next daemon startup: `--on-startup`

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/nightly-backup.tar --on-startup
pdm add https://example.com/nightly-backup.tar -S
```

`--on-startup`/`-S` marks the task `scheduled` with no fixed time; it only
starts (moves to `queued`) the next time the daemon process starts up —
useful for "run this the next time I reboot/restart the daemon" without
picking a specific clock time. Conflicts with `--at`.

Separately from this flag: any task that was already `queued` when the
daemon last stopped, or was `scheduled` via a plain `--on-startup` task,
automatically resumes into the queue on the next daemon start — see [Task
Lifecycle](/pdm/task-lifecycle/) for exactly which statuses survive a
restart and how.

## Checking what's scheduled

```bash
pdm list --status scheduled
```

Scheduled tasks show up in `pdm list` like any other, filterable via
`--status scheduled`/`-S` (see [Commands:
list](/pdm/commands-list/)) — note this is the *list* command's own
`--status` flag with its own short form, unrelated to `add`'s `--on-startup`
short form, since each command's flags are scoped to that command.
Guides.On-Complete Hooks:
# On-Complete Hooks

`--on-complete` runs a command once a task finishes (regardless of whether
it succeeded or failed — check `{status}` inside the command if you need to
branch on that).

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/big.iso --on-complete shutdown
pdm add https://example.com/big.iso -G shutdown
```

## Built-in commands

Five power-related actions are built in, resolved differently per platform:

| Alias | Linux | macOS | Windows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `shutdown` | `systemctl poweroff` | `shutdown -h now` | `shutdown /s /t 0` |
| `restart` | `systemctl reboot` | `shutdown -r now` | `shutdown /r /t 0` |
| `sleep` | `systemctl suspend` | `pmset sleepnow` | `rundll32.exe powrprof.dll,SetSuspendState 0,1,0` |
| `hibernate` | `systemctl hibernate` | `pmset sleepnow` | `shutdown /h` |
| `lock` | `loginctl lock-session` | `pmset displaysleepnow` | `rundll32.exe user32.dll,LockWorkStation` |

On Arch Linux (or any systemd-based distro), these resolve through
`systemctl`/`loginctl` as shown — no extra setup needed as long as your user
has permission to invoke them (typically via polkit).

## Custom aliases

Define your own in the config file's `onCompleteAliases` map, then reference
the alias name with `--on-complete`:

```yaml
onCompleteAliases:
  backup: "rsync -a {path} /mnt/backup/"
  notify-webhook: "curl -X POST -d 'status={status}&file={path}' https://example.com/hook"
  transcode: "ffmpeg -i {path} -c:v libx265 {path}.hevc.mkv"
```

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/video.mp4 --on-complete transcode
```

## Template variables

Both built-in and custom `--on-complete` commands have these substituted
before execution:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `{id}` | The task's id, e.g. `a3f9k2m1` |
| `{url}` | The source URL |
| `{path}` | The save path the file was written to |
| `{status}` | The final status name: `completed` or `failed` |

## Arbitrary shell commands

If `--on-complete`'s value isn't a built-in name or a key in
`onCompleteAliases`, it's run as-is through the platform shell (`/bin/sh -c`
on Linux/macOS, `cmd /c` on Windows):

```bash
pdm add https://example.com/file.iso --on-complete "echo Done: {path} >> ~/pdm-log.txt"
```

## Resolution order and failure handling

1. Check `onCompleteAliases` in the config file for an exact match.
2. Check the five built-in names above.
3. Otherwise, treat the value itself as a literal shell command.

The hook runs via `Process.run` (not awaited by the rest of pdm — it fires
and forgets) and any failure to launch it is silently swallowed, so a
misconfigured hook won't crash the daemon or mark the download itself as
failed; check your target command manually if it doesn't seem to be firing.

## Desktop notifications (separate from hooks)

Independently of `--on-complete`, set `notifications: true` in the config
file to get a desktop notification on every task completion/failure — via
`notify-send` on Linux, `osascript` on macOS, `msg` on Windows. This isn't a
hook and has no `{variables}`; it always shows a fixed "Download
complete"/"Download failed" title with the save path as the body.
Guides.Managing Tasks:
# Managing Tasks

Once a task exists (via `pdm add`), these commands operate on it by id.
Every one of `pause`, `resume`, `cancel`, and `remove` accepts **one or more
ids**, or `--all`/`-A` to apply to every task the action makes sense for.

## Listing tasks

```bash
pdm list
pdm ls                              # alias
pdm list --status downloading
pdm list --sort progress --reverse
pdm list --limit 10
```

See [Commands list](/pdm/commands-list/) for the full flag table (filter by
status, sort field, reverse, limit) and [Task
Lifecycle](/pdm/task-lifecycle/) for the full list of status values you can
filter on.

## Pausing and resuming

```bash
pdm pause a3f9k2m1
pdm pause a3f9k2m1 b7x2n9q4 c1d8e5f2    # multiple ids at once
pdm pause --all                          # every currently pausable task

pdm resume a3f9k2m1
pdm start a3f9k2m1                       # "start" is an alias for "resume"
```

Pausing an actively-downloading task cancels its in-flight HTTP requests but
keeps every segment's progress on disk, so `pdm resume` picks up exactly
where it left off (see [Multi-Connection Downloads &
Resume](/pdm/multi-connection-downloads-and-resume/)). A `queued` or
`scheduled` task can also be paused, which simply removes it from the
pending queue/schedule without ever starting it.

## Canceling and removing

```bash
pdm cancel a3f9k2m1
pdm remove a3f9k2m1
pdm rm a3f9k2m1                          # alias for remove
pdm remove a3f9k2m1 --delete-file        # also delete the partial/complete file on disk
pdm rm a3f9k2m1 -D                       # short form
```

`cancel` stops the task and marks it `canceled` but leaves its record (and
whatever bytes were written) around; `remove` additionally deletes the
task's record entirely (and, with `--delete-file`/`-D`, the file on disk
too). Both `cancel` and `remove` are treated as **destructive** actions.

## Confirmation prompts

`cancel` and `remove` prompt for confirmation when running in an interactive
terminal (i.e. `stdin` is a real TTY, not piped/redirected) and `--force`
wasn't passed:

```
remove (and delete file) 3 task(s): a3f9k2m1, b7x2n9q4, c1d8e5f2? [y/N]
```

- More than 5 ids are summarized as `id1, id2, id3, id4, id5, and N more`.
- Anything other than `y`/`yes` (case-insensitive) aborts with exit code 1
  and no tasks touched.
- Pass `--force`/`-F` to skip the prompt — required in scripts/cron, since
  there's no TTY to prompt on anyway (pdm skips the prompt automatically
  when `stdin` isn't a terminal, but `--force` makes that explicit and is
  recommended for anything unattended).

## Bulk operations with `--all`

```bash
pdm pause --all
pdm resume --all
pdm cancel --all --force
pdm remove --all --delete-file --force
```

`--all`/`-A` replaces the id list entirely — combining explicit ids with
`--all` isn't meaningful and `--all` takes precedence in that case. Which
tasks `--all` selects depends on the action, since each only makes sense for
certain statuses:

| Action | `--all` selects tasks with status |
| --- | --- |
| `pause` | `downloading` or `queued` |
| `resume` | `paused` or `failed` |
| `cancel` | anything **except** `completed` or `canceled` |
| `remove` | every task, regardless of status |

## Watching live progress

```bash
pdm watch a3f9k2m1
pdm watch a3f9k2m1 b7x2n9q4              # watch several concurrently
pdm watch a3f9k2m1 --no-bar
pdm watch a3f9k2m1 --interval 500
```

See [Commands watch](/pdm/commands-watch/) for `--interval` and `--no-bar`
in detail. Watching more than one id at once automatically switches to
plain-line output (as if `--no-bar` were passed) since multiple live bars
can't share a terminal cleanly, and each line is prefixed with `[id]` to
tell tasks apart.
Guides.Task Lifecycle:
# Task Lifecycle

Every task has exactly one status at a time, from this fixed set:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `queued` | Waiting for a free execution slot (`maxConcurrentTasks`) |
| `scheduled` | Waiting for its `--at` time, or for the daemon's next startup (`--on-startup`) |
| `probing` | Daemon is checking size/range support before starting segments |
| `downloading` | Actively transferring |
| `paused` | Stopped by `pdm pause`, with segment progress preserved |
| `verifying` | All segments finished; checksum is being computed (only if `--checksum` was given) |
| `completed` | Finished successfully (and checksum matched, if one was given) |
| `failed` | Ran out of retries, a checksum mismatched, or disk space was insufficient |
| `canceled` | Stopped by `pdm cancel` or `pdm remove`; partial file removed on cancel |

## Normal transitions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued
    [*] --> scheduled: --at / --every / --on-startup
    [*] --> paused: --start-paused
    scheduled --> queued: time reached / daemon started
    queued --> probing
    probing --> downloading
    downloading --> verifying: all segments done + --checksum given
    downloading --> completed: all segments done, no checksum
    verifying --> completed: checksum matches
    verifying --> failed: checksum mismatch
    downloading --> failed: retries exhausted
    downloading --> paused: pdm pause
    queued --> paused: pdm pause
    scheduled --> paused: pdm pause
    downloading --> canceled: pdm cancel / remove
    paused --> queued: pdm resume
    failed --> queued: pdm resume
    completed --> scheduled: --every (recurring task re-arms)
```

## Recurring tasks (`--every`)

A `completed` task created with `--every` doesn't stay `completed` — it's
immediately re-armed back to `scheduled` for its next run, with segments,
total size, and any previous error cleared, so `pdm list` shows it cycling
through `scheduled → queued → probing → downloading → completed →
scheduled → ...` indefinitely. See [Scheduling](/pdm/scheduling/#repeat-on-an-interval---every).

## What happens on daemon restart

When `pdmd` starts, it loads every saved task record and applies this
one-time correction pass before resuming normal operation:

- Any task that was `downloading` or `probing` when the daemon last stopped
  is moved to `paused` — it does **not** resume automatically, since the
  daemon can't be sure the interrupted state is clean. Run `pdm resume` (or
  `pdm resume --all`) to continue it.
- Any `scheduled` task whose schedule has `onStartup: true` (i.e. was added
  with `--on-startup`) is moved to `queued` and enters the normal queue
  immediately.
- Any task already `queued` re-enters the pending queue as-is.

This means a plain `queued` task (not `--on-startup`, not mid-download) does
survive a daemon restart and picks back up on its own — it's specifically
the "was actively transferring" and "was scheduled for later" cases that
need an explicit nudge or a matching schedule condition.

## Queue ordering

Within `queued`, tasks start in **descending priority** order
(`--priority`/`-y`, default `0`; higher runs first), up to
`maxConcurrentTasks` running at once. Same-priority tasks are otherwise
served in the order they became queued.

## `error` field

`failed` and `canceled` tasks may carry a human-readable `error` string
(visible via `pdm list --json` or `pdm history --json`) — e.g. `"HTTP 403
for segment 2"`, `"Checksum mismatch"`, `"Not enough disk space: need N
bytes, have M"`, or `"Incomplete download"` for a generic
retries-exhausted failure with no more specific cause recorded.
Guides.Daemon and Service:
# Daemon and Service

`pdmd` is the background process that runs your downloads. `pdm daemon`
manages its lifecycle.

## Starting and stopping manually

```bash
pdm daemon start          # start it if not already running
pdm daemon start --foreground   # run attached, for debugging — blocks until SIGINT/SIGTERM
pdm daemon stop
pdm daemon status
```

`pdm daemon start` (without `--foreground`) is mostly redundant day-to-day —
`pdm add`, `pdm list`, and every other command auto-spawn the daemon on
first contact anyway, unless you pass `--no-spawn`/`-n`. It's most useful
for confirming the daemon *can* start cleanly, or right after installing.

`pdm daemon start --foreground` runs the daemon directly in your terminal
(no auto-spawn, no detaching) until you send `SIGINT` (Ctrl-C) or, on
Linux/macOS, `SIGTERM`. Useful when debugging daemon behavior directly or
running it under a supervisor other than the built-in service integration.

## Auto-starting at login

```bash
pdm daemon enable     # installs a login-time auto-start entry
pdm daemon disable     # removes it
```

On Arch Linux (or any systemd user session), `enable` writes a unit file to
`~/.config/systemd/user/pdmd.service`:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=pdm download manager daemon

[Service]
ExecStart=<path-to-pdmd>
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
```

then runs `systemctl --user daemon-reload` followed by `systemctl --user
enable --now pdmd.service`. If your user session doesn't linger past logout
by default, enable lingering so the daemon keeps running even when you're
not logged in interactively:

```bash
loginctl enable-linger psdk
```

`pdm daemon disable` reverses this: `systemctl --user disable --now
pdmd.service`, deletes the unit file, and reloads the systemd user daemon.

On macOS, `enable`/`disable` install/remove a launchd agent at
`~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.pdm.daemon.plist` (`RunAtLoad` +
`KeepAlive`); on Windows, they register/remove a logon Scheduled Task named
`pdm daemon` via `schtasks`.

## No-spawn mode

```bash
pdm list --no-spawn
pdm list -n
```

`--no-spawn`/`-n` is a **global** flag (available on every command) that
makes pdm fail with a connection error instead of auto-starting `pdmd` when
it isn't already running — useful in scripts where you want to explicitly
control daemon lifecycle rather than have it start implicitly on first use.

## Connecting to a non-default daemon

```bash
pdm list --socket-path /tmp/other-pdm.sock
pdm list --daemon-host 192.0.2.10 --daemon-port 7500   # Windows TCP transport
```

`--socket-path`/`-s` (Linux/macOS) and `--daemon-host`/`-H` +
`--daemon-port`/`-P` (Windows) are global flags that override the
config-derived address for a single command invocation — handy for pointing
at a daemon running under a different user or in a container, without
editing the config file.
Guides.Shell Completion:
# Shell Completion

```bash
pdm completion            # auto-detects from $SHELL
pdm completion bash
pdm completion zsh
```

## What makes it "smart"

Unlike a static word list, pdm's completion scripts are generated straight
from pdm's own internal flag definitions (the same source `pdm help` reads
from), so they can't drift out of sync with the actual CLI:

- Only offers flags that are still legal given what's already typed —
  mutually exclusive pairs like `--foreground`/`--background`,
  `--file`/`--output`, and `--at`/`--on-startup` won't both be suggested
  once one is typed, and a flag already used isn't offered a second time.
- Fills in the actual legal values for flags with a fixed choice set, e.g.
  `--status`, `--sort`, `--format`, `--theme`, `--on-complete`.
- Completes file paths for path-taking flags (`--output`, `--file`,
  `--cookie-file`, `--config`, `--socket-path`).
- Completes live task ids for `pause`/`resume`/`cancel`/`remove`/`watch` by
  quietly running `pdm list --json` in the background.
- Completes sub-actions for `daemon` (`start`/`stop`/`status`/`enable`/
  `disable`), `completion` (`bash`/`zsh`), and `config` (`dump`).

On **zsh**, every suggestion — commands, flags, values, actions, and task
ids — comes with an inline description. Bash completion can't show
descriptions (a shell limitation), so it's value/context-aware but
word-only.

## Install locations

| Flag | Bash target | Zsh target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (default, system-wide) | `/usr/share/bash-completion/completions/pdm` | `/usr/share/zsh/site-functions/_pdm` |
| `--user`/`-u` | `~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/pdm` | `~/.local/share/zsh/site-functions/_pdm` |

```bash
sudo pdm completion bash          # system-wide, needs root
pdm completion bash --user        # per-user, no root needed
pdm completion zsh --print        # print the script instead of installing it
```

If the system-wide path isn't writable, pdm prints the exact `sudo` command
to re-run plus the `--user` alternative rather than failing silently:

```
Could not write to /usr/share/bash-completion/completions/pdm (permission denied).
Run this to install system-wide:
  sudo pdm completion bash
Or install it for your user only:
  pdm completion bash --user
```

`--print`/`-p` and `--user`/`-u` are mutually exclusive — printing to stdout
doesn't install anywhere, so a target directory is meaningless in that mode.

## After installing

```bash
# bash — reload your shell, or:
source /usr/share/bash-completion/completions/pdm

# zsh — reload your shell, or:
autoload -U compinit && compinit
```
Guides.Themes:
# Themes

pdm ships three color themes for progress bars and status text.

```bash
pdm --theme catppuccin add https://example.com/file.iso
pdm -T rainbow watch a3f9k2m1
```

`--theme`/`-T` is a **global** flag, so it goes before the command like any
other global flag, and can also be set persistently via the `theme` key in
the config file. Accepted values: `default`, `rainbow`, `catppuccin`.

## `default`

Plain ANSI colors: cyan progress bar, green success, red error, yellow
warning, cyan info, dim/gray muted text, bold for headers.

## `rainbow`

The progress bar cycles through 8 colors (`196, 208, 220, 46, 51, 21, 93,
201` — 256-color ANSI codes) character by character as it fills; status text
uses bright variants of the default palette's colors.

## `catppuccin`

Uses the [Catppuccin](https://catppuccin.com) Mocha palette via 24-bit true
color escape codes:

| Role | Color |
| --- | --- |
| Progress bar (filled) | Mauve |
| Progress bar (empty) | Overlay |
| Success | Green |
| Error | Red (Catppuccin's "Red"/Maroon-adjacent) |
| Warning | Yellow |
| Info | Sky |
| Muted | Overlay |
| Bold/headers | Text, bolded |

Needs a true-color-capable terminal to render as intended (most modern
terminal emulators on Arch, including foot, alacritty, kitty, and
GNOME/Konsole's default profiles, support this).

## Disabling color entirely

```bash
pdm --no-color list
pdm -N list
```

`--no-color`/`-N` is a global flag that forces plain, uncolored output
regardless of theme — useful for logging to a file or a non-ANSI terminal.
Color is also automatically disabled when stdout isn't a real terminal
(e.g. piped into `less` or redirected to a file) or when `color: false` is
set in the config file, even without `--no-color`.
Guides.Proxies and Networking:
# Proxies and Networking

## Basic proxy

```bash
pdm add <url> --proxy http://127.0.0.1:8080
pdm add <url> -p http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

`--proxy`/`-p` sets an HTTP proxy for that task; set `proxy` in the config
file to make it the default for every task that doesn't override it. A
matching [rule](/pdm/configuration/#per-url-rules)'s `proxy` field takes
priority over the config default but is itself overridden by an explicit
`--proxy` flag on `add`.

## Proxy authentication

```bash
pdm add <url> --proxy http://proxy.example.com:8080 \
  --proxy-user psdk --proxy-pass hunter2
pdm add <url> -p http://proxy.example.com:8080 -Q psdk -W hunter2
```

`--proxy-user`/`-Q` and `--proxy-pass`/`-W` send HTTP Basic auth to the
proxy itself (separate from `--auth-user`/`--auth-pass`, which authenticates
to the destination server). Also settable as `proxyUser`/`proxyPass` in the
config file.

## Bypassing the proxy for specific hosts

There's no per-task flag for this — set `proxyBypass` in the config file as
a list of hostnames:

```yaml
proxy: "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
proxyBypass:
  - internal.corp.example
  - localhost
```

A host matches if it equals an entry exactly, or is a subdomain of one
(`files.internal.corp.example` matches `internal.corp.example`). Matching
hosts connect `DIRECT`, bypassing the proxy entirely.

## TLS certificate verification

```bash
pdm add <url> --insecure
pdm add <url> -i
```

`--insecure`/`-i` disables TLS certificate verification for that task —
useful for self-signed certs on internal servers, but it defeats
protection against man-in-the-middle attacks, so avoid it for anything
over an untrusted network. Also settable as `insecure: true` in the config
file for a blanket default (not recommended globally).

## Redirects

```bash
pdm add <url> --max-redirects 10
pdm add <url> -m 10
```

`--max-redirects`/`-m` caps how many HTTP redirects pdm will follow before
giving up (default `5`, from config `maxRedirects`).

## Timeouts

```bash
pdm add <url> --timeout 60
pdm add <url> -t 60
```

`--timeout`/`-t` sets the connection/read timeout in seconds (default `30`,
from config `timeout`) — applied as the underlying HTTP client's connection
timeout for that task.

## Custom headers and User-Agent

```bash
pdm add <url> --header "X-Custom: value" --user-agent "psdk-pdm/3.1.0"
```

See [Adding Downloads](/pdm/adding-downloads/#headers-auth-and-cookies) for
the full rundown, including cookies and Basic auth.

# Troubleshooting

## "Duplicate of existing task ... (same url or save path)"

`pdm add` refuses to queue a URL (or inferred/explicit save path) that
matches an existing non-completed, non-canceled task. Either let the
existing task finish/cancel it first, or pass `--allow-duplicate`/`-D` if
you genuinely want two copies. See [Adding
Downloads](/pdm/adding-downloads/#duplicate-detection).

## "--output can only be used with a single url"

`--output`/`-o` names one exact file, which is meaningless when adding
several URLs at once (they'd all collide on the same path). Drop `--output`
and let pdm infer names from each URL, or add them one at a time.

## "--output cannot be used with --file"

Same underlying reason: `--file` (batch mode) adds many URLs with names
inferred per-line; `--output` names a single file. Drop one or the other.

## "Not enough disk space: need N bytes, have M"

pdm checks free space against the file's known total size (minus
already-downloaded bytes, for a resume) before writing. Free up space, or
set `checkDiskSpace: false` in the config file to skip the check (not
recommended — you'll just get a filesystem-level write error later instead
of a clean one up front).

## "Checksum mismatch"

The downloaded file's hash didn't match the `--checksum` you supplied.
Double-check the expected `algo:hex` value came from a trusted source and
matches the exact file at that URL — a checksum mismatch usually means
either the wrong value was pasted, or the download was corrupted/tampered
with in transit and should be re-run.

## "Lost connection to the pdm daemon" (during `watch`/foreground `add`)

The daemon process stopped or crashed mid-download (e.g. `pdm daemon stop`
ran concurrently, or the process was killed). Check `pdm daemon status`;
restart it and `pdm resume <id>` to continue where the task left off —
segment progress up to the disconnect is preserved. This exact scenario
used to hang the calling `pdm` process indefinitely; now it always exits
with a clear error, so if you see this cleanly reported, that's the fix
working as intended rather than a new problem.

## `pdm daemon enable` fails, or auto-spawn silently does nothing

Usually means `pdmd` can't be located next to the `pdm` binary. This
specifically affects compiled installs where the two binaries got separated
(e.g. only `pdm` was copied somewhere, or a custom install script only
grabbed one binary). Set `PDMD_PATH` explicitly to point at the `pdmd`
executable — see [Environment Variables](/pdm/environment-variables/).

## Permission denied installing shell completion or the binaries themselves

Both the release installer and `pdm completion` default to system-wide
locations that need root. Either re-run with `sudo` as the tool itself
suggests, or add `--user`/`-u` to install into your own home directory
instead — see [Shell Completion](/pdm/shell-completion/#install-locations)
and [Getting Started](/pdm/getting-started/#1-install).

## `pdm version` prints the wrong version after a manual build

If you compiled `bin/pdm.dart` yourself without `--define=PDM_VERSION=...`,
pdm falls back to reading `pubspec.yaml` relative to `Platform.script` —
which only resolves correctly under `dart run`, not from a compiled
executable with no `pubspec.yaml` next to it. Compile with
`--define=PDM_VERSION=<version>` to bake the string in, as the official
release workflow does. See [Building from
source](/pdm/requirements-and-platforms/#building-from-source).

## Nothing happens when a `--on-complete` hook should have fired

Hook failures are swallowed silently by design (a bad hook shouldn't crash
the daemon or mark a good download as failed). Test the resolved command
manually in a shell first, and double check `{id}`/`{url}`/`{path}`/
`{status}` substitution matches what you expect — see [On-Complete
Hooks](/pdm/on-complete-hooks/).

API Reference.CLI Overview:
# CLI Overview

```
pdm <command> [flags]
```

Every command accepts these global flags in addition to its own. Global
flags can appear anywhere on the command line (before or interleaved with
the command's own flags/positionals).

## Global flags

| Short | Long | Kind | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-v` | `--verbose` | flag | Print extra diagnostic output |
| `-q` | `--quiet` | flag | Suppress non-essential output |
| `-j` | `--json` | flag | Machine-readable JSON output |
| `-H` | `--daemon-host` | string | Daemon TCP host (**Windows only**) |
| `-P` | `--daemon-port` | string | Daemon TCP port (**Windows only**) |
| `-s` | `--socket-path` | string (path) | Daemon Unix socket path (**Linux/macOS only**) |
| `-n` | `--no-spawn` | flag | Fail instead of auto-spawning the daemon |
| `-g` | `--config` | string (path) | Path to config file |
| `-T` | `--theme` | string (choice) | Progress/output theme: `default`, `rainbow`, `catppuccin` |
| `-N` | `--no-color` | flag | Disable ANSI colors |
| `-h` | `--help` | flag | Show help for this command |

`-h`/`--help` is checked before strict flag parsing, so `pdm <command>
--help` (or with any other, even invalid, flags alongside it) always shows
that command's help instead of a parse error.

## Commands

| Command | Aliases | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `add` | | Add and start one or more downloads |
| `list` | `ls` | List all tasks |
| `pause` | | Pause one or more tasks |
| `resume` | `start` | Resume one or more paused/queued tasks |
| `cancel` | | Cancel one or more tasks |
| `remove` | `rm` | Remove one or more tasks |
| `watch` | | Attach a live progress view to one or more tasks |
| `daemon` | | Manage the background daemon |
| `config` | | Manage the config file |
| `history` | | Show completed/failed download history |
| `completion` | | Install or print a shell completion script |
| `version` | | Print the pdm version |
| `help` | | Show help, or help for one command |

Run `pdm help` for this same table at any time, or `pdm help <command>` /
`pdm <command> --help` for one command's full flag list, including any
fixed value choices inline.

## Flag precedence

For any option settable in more than one place, the order is:

1. The flag on the command line (highest priority).
2. A matching [rule](/pdm/configuration/#per-url-rules) in the config file
   (only applies to `add`-time task options, and only for fields a rule can
   override).
3. The corresponding key in the config file.
4. pdm's built-in default (lowest priority).

## Unknown flags and typos

An unrecognized `--flag` suggests the closest known flag name by edit
distance:

```
$ pdm add <url> --conections 8
Unknown flag --conections. Did you mean --connections?
```

The same applies to unknown commands and to `pdm help <command>` /
`pdm <command> --help` for a mistyped command name.

## Exit codes

pdm doesn't define a large custom exit-code table — commands return `0` on
success and `1` on any failure (a parse error, a rejected request, a
task-level failure in `--foreground` mode, an aborted confirmation prompt,
etc.). For bulk operations (multiple ids, or `--all`), the exit code is `1`
if **any** individual operation failed, even if others succeeded — check the
printed per-id `ok`/error summary, or use `--json` and inspect it
programmatically, to distinguish partial from total failure.

## Machine-readable output

```bash
pdm list --json
pdm history --json
pdm add <url> --json    # background mode only; prints the daemon's response object
```

`--json`/`-j` is a global flag, but it only changes the output of commands
that print structured data (`list`, `history`, background `add`) — commands
whose output is inherently a live progress display (`watch`, foreground
`add`) or plain confirmation text aren't affected by it.
API Reference.Commands add:
# Commands: `add`

```
pdm add <url> [<url> ...] [flags]
```

Add and start one or more downloads. See [Adding
Downloads](/pdm/adding-downloads/) and [Multi-Connection Downloads &
Resume](/pdm/multi-connection-downloads-and-resume/) for guided walkthroughs
of these flags in context.

| Short | Long | Kind | Config fallback | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-o` | `--output` | string (path) | | Save path for the downloaded file (single-url only); conflicts with `--file` |
| `-c` | `--connections` | string (int) | `connections` | Number of concurrent connections/segments |
| `-f` | `--foreground` | flag | | Block in this process with a live progress bar; conflicts with `--background` |
| `-b` | `--background` | flag | | Run via the daemon and return immediately (default); conflicts with `--foreground` |
| `-e` | `--header` | string, repeatable | | Custom header `"Key: Value"` |
| `-u` | `--user-agent` | string | | Custom User-Agent header |
| `-R` | `--referer` | string | | Referer header |
| `-C` | `--cookie` | string | | Inline cookie string `"key=value; key2=value2"` |
| `-J` | `--cookie-file` | string (path) | | Netscape-format cookie file (wins over `--cookie`) |
| `-p` | `--proxy` | string | `proxy` | HTTP proxy URL |
| `-Q` | `--proxy-user` | string | `proxyUser` | Proxy basic-auth username |
| `-W` | `--proxy-pass` | string | `proxyPass` | Proxy basic-auth password |
| `-r` | `--retries` | string (int) | `retries` | Retry attempts per segment |
| `-d` | `--retry-delay` | string (int, ms) | `retryDelay` | Delay between retries in milliseconds |
| `-L` | `--linear-retries` | flag | | Disable exponential backoff between retries |
| `-t` | `--timeout` | string (int, sec) | `timeout` | Connection/read timeout in seconds |
| `-l` | `--speed-limit` | string | `speedLimit` | Max download speed, e.g. `2M`, `500K` |
| `-k` | `--checksum` | string | | Expected checksum `"algo:hex"`, e.g. `sha256:abc123` |
| `-U` | `--auth-user` | string | | Basic auth username |
| `-w` | `--auth-pass` | string | | Basic auth password |
| `-i` | `--insecure` | flag | `insecure` | Skip TLS certificate verification |
| `-O` | `--overwrite` | flag | | Overwrite an existing file at the save path |
| `-x` | `--start-paused` | flag | | Add the task without starting it |
| `-y` | `--priority` | string (int) | | Queue priority (higher runs first) |
| `-m` | `--max-redirects` | string (int) | `maxRedirects` | Maximum redirects to follow |
| `-a` | `--at` | string | | Schedule start time: ISO date/time, `"HH:mm"`, or `"+<duration>"`; conflicts with `--on-startup` |
| `-E` | `--every` | string | | Repeat this download on an interval, e.g. `1d`, `6h`, `30m` |
| `-S` | `--on-startup` | flag | | Defer this download until the daemon next starts; conflicts with `--at` |
| `-G` | `--on-complete` | string (choice*) | | Command/alias to run when the download finishes |
| `-D` | `--allow-duplicate` | flag | | Allow adding a task with a duplicate url/save path |
| `-B` | `--file` | string (path) | | Batch-add every URL (one per line) from this file; conflicts with `--output` |

\* `--on-complete`'s built-in choices are `shutdown`, `restart`, `sleep`,
`hibernate`, `lock` — but any value is accepted, since it may also refer to
a custom key in the config file's `onCompleteAliases`, or be a literal shell
command. See [On-Complete Hooks](/pdm/on-complete-hooks/).

## Positional arguments

One or more URLs, unless `--file` is given (in which case positionals are
ignored and URLs are read from the file instead). At least one URL — from
either source — is required.

## Byte size format (`--speed-limit`)

`<number>[K|M|G]`, case-insensitive, binary multiples (`K` = 1024 bytes,
`M` = 1024² bytes, `G` = 1024³ bytes). A bare number with no suffix is
treated as an exact byte count. Examples: `500K`, `2M`, `1.5G`, `1048576`.

## Duration format (`--every`)

`<number><unit>` with no space, unit one of `ms`, `s`, `m`, `h`, `d`.
Examples: `30m`, `6h`, `1d`, `500ms`.

## `--at` format

See the table in [Scheduling](/pdm/scheduling/#start-at-a-specific-time---at)
for the three accepted forms (ISO date/time, `HH:mm`, `+<duration>`).

## Header format (`--header`)

`"Key: Value"` — everything before the first `:` is the header name
(trimmed), everything after is the value (trimmed). Repeat the flag for
multiple headers.

## Checksum format (`--checksum`)

`"algo:hex"` where `algo` is one of `md5`, `sha1`, `sha256`, `sha512`.
API Reference.Commands list:
# Commands: `list`

```
pdm list [flags]
```

Alias: `ls`. List all tasks known to the daemon, as a table (or JSON with
`--json`).

| Short | Long | Kind | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-S` | `--status` | string (choice) | Filter by status |
| `-t` | `--sort` | string (choice) | Sort field: `created`, `updated`, `progress`, `name` |
| `-R` | `--reverse` | flag | Reverse the sort order |
| `-L` | `--limit` | string (int) | Maximum number of rows to show |

## `--status` choices

`queued`, `scheduled`, `probing`, `downloading`, `paused`, `verifying`,
`completed`, `failed`, `canceled` — the same set documented in full in [Task
Lifecycle](/pdm/task-lifecycle/).

## `--sort` fields

| Value | Sorts by |
| --- | --- |
| `created` (default) | `createdAt`, ascending |
| `updated` | `updatedAt`, ascending |
| `progress` | Fraction complete (`downloadedBytes / totalBytes`), ascending |
| `name` | Save path, lexicographic |

`--reverse`/`-R` flips whichever order `--sort` produces (applied after
sorting, before `--limit`). `--limit`/`-L` truncates the result to the first
N rows after sorting/filtering/reversing.

## Output

Without `--json`: a formatted table with status-colored rows (per the
active [theme](/pdm/themes/)). With `--json`/`-j`: the full array of task
records as JSON, each with the same shape documented in [Using pdm as a Dart
Library](/pdm/using-pdm-as-a-dart-library/#taskrecord).
API Reference.Commands Task Actions:
# Commands: `pause` / `resume` / `cancel` / `remove`

```
pdm pause <id> [<id> ...] [flags]
pdm resume <id> [<id> ...] [flags]     # alias: start
pdm cancel <id> [<id> ...] [flags]
pdm remove <id> [<id> ...] [flags]     # alias: rm
```

These four share one underlying implementation and one flag set, plus one
extra flag specific to `remove`.

## Shared flags

| Short | Long | Kind | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-A` | `--all` | flag | Apply to every matching task instead of the given ids |
| `-F` | `--force` | flag | Skip confirmation prompts |

## `remove`-only flag

| Short | Long | Kind | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-D` | `--delete-file` | flag | Also delete the downloaded file |

## Positional arguments

One or more task ids, unless `--all`/`-A` is given (in which case
positionals are ignored). Duplicate ids in the list are deduplicated
automatically (order-preserving).

## Which tasks `--all` matches

See the table in [Managing Tasks](/pdm/managing-tasks/#bulk-operations-with---all)
— each action only applies `--all` to the statuses that action makes sense
for (e.g. `--all` with `pause` only touches `downloading`/`queued` tasks,
not ones already `paused` or `completed`).

## Confirmation prompts

`cancel` and `remove` are destructive and prompt for confirmation when
`stdin` is an interactive terminal and `--force`/`-F` wasn't passed. See
[Managing Tasks](/pdm/managing-tasks/#confirmation-prompts) for the exact
prompt format and batching behavior for long id lists.

## Per-id result reporting

For more than one id, each command prints a per-id success/failure line as
it goes, then a summary count (`N/M succeeded.`) at the end. The command's
own exit code is `1` if any individual id failed, `0` only if all
succeeded.
API Reference.Commands watch:
# Commands: `watch`

```
pdm watch <id> [<id> ...] [flags]
```

Attach a live progress view to one or more tasks, streaming updates from the
daemon until each watched task reaches a terminal status (`completed`,
`failed`, or `canceled`).

| Short | Long | Kind | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-I` | `--interval` | string (int, ms) | Refresh interval in milliseconds |
| `-B` | `--no-bar` | flag | Print plain progress lines instead of a bar |

## Positional arguments

One or more task ids (deduplicated, order-preserving).

## Single vs. multiple ids

- **One id**: renders a live-updating progress bar (unless `--no-bar`) using
  the active [theme](/pdm/themes/), refreshed at most every `--interval`
  milliseconds (default `200`), with a final summary line once the task
  reaches a terminal status.
- **More than one id**: automatically switches to plain-line output as if
  `--no-bar` were passed (multiple live bars can't coexist cleanly in one
  terminal), watches all of them concurrently over separate daemon
  connections, and prefixes every line with `[id]` to distinguish tasks.
  Exits once every watched task reaches a terminal status; overall exit
  code is `0` only if all of them succeeded.

## Connection loss

If the daemon connection drops while watching, `pdm watch` prints
`"Lost connection to the pdm daemon"` (prefixed with `[id]` in multi-watch
mode) and exits with code `1`, rather than hanging indefinitely. See
[Troubleshooting](/pdm/troubleshooting/#lost-connection-to-the-pdm-daemon-during-watchforeground-add).
API Reference.Commands Misc:
# Commands Misc

`daemon`, `config`, `history`, `completion`, plus the top-level `version`
and `help` commands, which take no flags of their own.

## `pdm daemon`

```
pdm daemon <start|stop|status|enable|disable> [flags]
```

| Short | Long | Kind | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-f` | `--foreground` | flag | Run the daemon attached, for debugging (only with `start`) |

### Actions

| Action | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `start` | Start the daemon (spawns it if not already running) |
| `stop` | Stop the running daemon |
| `status` | Check whether the daemon is running |
| `enable` | Start the daemon automatically at login |
| `disable` | Remove the auto-start entry |

See [Daemon and Service](/pdm/daemon-and-service/) for platform-specific
detail on `enable`/`disable`.

## `pdm config dump`

```
pdm config dump [flags]
```

| Short | Long | Kind | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-f` | `--format` | string (choice) | Output format: `yaml`, `toml`, `json` |
| `-o` | `--output` | string (path) | Write to file instead of stdout |
| `-F` | `--force` | flag | Overwrite an existing file |

### Actions

| Action | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `dump` | Print (or write) the default config file |

`dump` is currently the only `config` sub-action. Without `--output`,
prints the rendered default config to stdout in the chosen `--format`
(default `yaml`) — it does not read or merge your existing config file,
it always renders pdm's built-in defaults. With `--output`/`-o`, writes to
that path instead, inferring the format from the file extension unless
`--format` is given explicitly; fails if the file already exists unless
`--force`/`-F` is passed.

## `pdm history`

```
pdm history [flags]
```

| Short | Long | Kind | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-L` | `--limit` | string (int) | Maximum number of entries to show |
| `-C` | `--clear` | flag | Clear the history log |

Shows a persistent log of every task that reached `completed` or `failed`,
newest first, stored as newline-delimited JSON at
`<state dir>/history.jsonl` (`~/.local/state/pdm/history.jsonl` by default
on Linux). Each line is appended when a task finishes, independent of the
task record itself (so history survives `pdm remove`). `--clear`/`-C`
deletes the log file entirely; combine with `--json`/`-j` for a
machine-readable array instead of the formatted table (with a totals row —
combined size and average speed across shown entries — omitted in JSON
mode).

## `pdm completion`

```
pdm completion <bash|zsh> [flags]
```

| Short | Long | Kind | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-p` | `--print` | flag | Print the script to stdout instead of installing it; conflicts with `--user` |
| `-u` | `--user` | flag | Install to the per-user completion dir instead of system-wide; conflicts with `--print` |

### Actions

| Action | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `bash` | Install/print the bash completion script |
| `zsh` | Install/print the zsh completion script |

With no action given, auto-detects bash/zsh from `$SHELL`. See [Shell
Completion](/pdm/shell-completion/) for install-location and permission
details, and note that on Windows the script is always printed (as if
`--print` were passed) since automatic install is only supported on
Linux/macOS.

## `pdm version`

```
pdm version
```

Takes no flags. Prints pdm's version string and exits. In a release binary
this is baked in at compile time via `--define=PDM_VERSION=<version>`; when
run via `dart run` during development with no baked-in value, it falls back
to reading the `version` field from `pubspec.yaml` next to the script, and
finally to a hardcoded fallback string if even that can't be read.

## `pdm help`

```
pdm help [<command>]
```

Takes no flags. With no argument, prints the same command table shown by
running `pdm` with no arguments at all. With a command name (including an
alias, e.g. `pdm help rm`), prints that command's full usage line, summary,
aliases, sub-actions (if any), and complete flag list with inline value
choices — the same content `pdm <command> --help` shows.
API Reference.Configuration Schema:
# Configuration Schema

A field-by-field schema of the config file, for reference alongside the
narrative [Configuration](/pdm/configuration/) guide. All keys are optional;
shown types match how [`pdata`](https://pub.dev/packages/pdata) will parse
each YAML/TOML/JSON value.

## Top level

```
connections:          int              (default 4)
maxConcurrentTasks:    int              (default 3)
retries:               int              (default 3)
retryDelay:            int (ms)         (default 1000)
retryBackoff:          bool             (default true)
timeout:               int (sec)        (default 30)
speedLimit:            int (bytes/s) | null   (default null)
globalSpeedLimit:      int (bytes/s) | null   (default null)
maxRedirects:          int              (default 5)
insecure:              bool             (default false)
downloadDir:           string (path)    (default "~/Downloads")
theme:                 "default" | "rainbow" | "catppuccin"   (default "default")
color:                 bool             (default true)
daemonHost:            string           (default "127.0.0.1")      # Windows only
daemonPort:            int              (default 7420)             # Windows only
socketPath:            string (path)    (default "~/.local/state/pdm/pdm.sock")  # Linux/macOS only
proxy:                 string | null    (default null)
proxyUser:             string | null    (default null)
proxyPass:             string | null    (default null)
proxyBypass:           list<string>     (default [])
onCompleteAliases:     map<string, string>   (default {})
rules:                 list<Rule>       (default [])
notifications:         bool             (default false)
checkDiskSpace:        bool             (default true)
```

## `Rule` object (entries in `rules`)

```
pattern:       string (regex, required)     # also accepts "match" as a legacy alias
saveDir:       string (path), optional      # also accepts "dir" as a legacy alias
connections:   int, optional
proxy:         string, optional
speedLimit:    int (bytes/s), optional
headers:       map<string, string>, optional
onComplete:    string, optional
```

Only `pattern` is required; every other field falls through to the
non-rule value (flag/config/default) when omitted. Rules are evaluated in
list order and the **first match wins** — later rules are not merged in on
top, so put more specific patterns before more general ones if that
matters for your setup.

## Notes on types

- Any `int (bytes/s)` field in the config file (`speedLimit`,
  `globalSpeedLimit`, a rule's `speedLimit`) is a **raw byte count**, not a
  `K`/`M`/`G`-suffixed string like the `--speed-limit` CLI flag accepts —
  convert manually (e.g. `10485760` for 10 MiB/s) when writing the config
  file directly.
- Path-shaped string fields (`downloadDir`, `socketPath`, a rule's
  `saveDir`) have `~` expanded to the home directory at load time.
- `proxyBypass` entries are bare hostnames (no scheme, no port) —
  subdomains of a listed host also bypass automatically.
